newsitem.title: CANADA: CIBC sees consolidation in Canada's bank sector.
newsitem.headline: CIBC sees consolidation in Canada's bank sector.

text.p: Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce, the country's second largest bank, expects the consolidation in world banking to sweep through Canada's highly concentrated bank sector in the next five years.
"I think the next five years will be a critical period," Al Flood, CIBC chairman and chief executive officer told Reuters in an interview.
While Europe, Japan and the United States have all seen massive bank mergers in recent years, Canadian bankers have watched their world rankings slide sharply.

Canada's five major banks, including CIBC, are already teaming up to share back-office operations, partly to offset the high cost of electronic banking services. Some observers believe these back-door alliances are the first step toward bigger mergers.
CIBC is taking the lead with an ambitious plan to revamp traditional bank branches by weaning customers off tellers and onto electronic banking.

"Economies of scale and size become a major factor to compete in the global market place. With the huge investments that have to be made in technology and communication it may well be that the Canadian banks have to consolidate," said Flood.
Canadian laws at present discourage bank mergers by limiting individual investors to a 10 percent stake in domestic banks.
Canada's big five banks dominate regular banking, trusts and the brokerage trade and, despite recent setbacks, continue to lobby for better access to insurance and auto leasing.
The highly profitable banks also face mounting hostility from consumers angry about high service fees and from industry rivals who fear the banks' growing power.

CIBC on Thursday reported a third-quarter profit of C$336 million ($245 million) in the period ended July 31 -- up 24 percent from a year ago. All five major banks are on track for a third straight year of record earnings.
Nevertheless, Flood said CIBC is developing contingency plans for a further shakeout in Canadian banking.
"We do a lot of what-if scenarios. What if changes take place in the United States or what happens if competitors here make a move. It's good strategic thinking," he said.
Analysts also predict that mergers are inevitable if Canadian banks are to remain competitive against bigger foreign competitors in overseas markets.

"We expect that ultimately bank mergers have got to come if the Canadian banking system is going remain competitive with what's taking place in the global environment," said Nigel Heath, a senior analyst with Dominion Bond Rating Service.
In a study of Canada's banks, Dominion Bond concluded that overcapacity is restricting the industry's long-term profitability and growth.
The banks are hampered by oversized branch networks, which make it more costly to introduce new electronic delivery services, the debt rating agency said.
Competition is also a major threat with foreign and Canadian non-bank financial companies planning forays into the key C$90 billion ($65 billion)-a-year retail banking market.

"There is only so much revenue out there and other competitors are going to come into the marketplace. They will open branchless banks and will drive down fees so it's going to be critical for the winners to manage their overheads successfully," Flood said.
Earlier this summer the Dutch bank ING Groep N.V. announced it plans to offer an electronic, branchless bank -- also called a virtual bank -- in Canada.

A virtual bank is also being planned by a consortium that includes Canadian financial services companies, Trimark Financial Corp., AGF Management Ltd. and Citibank Canada, a unit of U.S.-based Citicorp.
In a bid to take the lead in electronic banking, CIBC is investing heavily to upgrade its branch network with more automated teller machines, telephone amd computer banking.
Billing it as the branch of the future, CIBC said recent test projects show the average transaction time fell to 15 seconds from over four minutes.
CIBC is working with vendors to supply more sophisticated machines that can deliver Canadian and U.S. cash, travellers checks and products like mutual funds.
"Once people use these services they never go back to the old traditional way of banking. Our challenge is how do we manage overhead," Flood said.
